frameworks.name: Hourly-Rate Purchase Test
frameworks.definition: Evaluate any purchase by converting its cost into work hours at your post-tax hourly rate, then ask: would I voluntarily work those hours just to acquire this item?

claims.text: When you calculate how many hours of post-tax work a purchase requires, the pain of that trade becomes salient, and you stop making purchases you wouldn't voluntarily work for. Alex Hormozi, working at $6 per hour after taxes, realized a $13 lunch cost two hours of his shift—and when framed as 'would I work two hours for this sandwich?', the behavior changed immediately.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Making the time-cost of a purchase explicit (converting dollars to work hours) triggers loss aversion and rational decision-making instead of impulse spending.

numbers.axis: hourly earnings to purchase cost ratio

bounded_by: The logic scales: at $100/hr post-tax, a $500-1000 purchase requires 5-10 hours of work, which reframes the same spend decision

claims.text: Saving money itself does not directly generate wealth, but it enables capital accumulation. Capital accumulation allows longer time horizons for decision-making, which enables taking on bigger risks. Bigger risks produce bigger returns, which is how capital compounds.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Savings → capital available → ability to hold longer vision → bigger risk-taking → larger returns → compounding effect
bounded_by: Saving money alone does not make money; it is a prerequisite for the subsequent behaviors that do

claims.text: When cash comes in only through one known source (e.g., a $2,000/month personal training client paying in cash), the easy way to enforce a budget is to only spend what is physically in your wallet and only replenish it as that client pays. This creates an automatic, rule-based spending ceiling that requires no willpower.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Single revenue stream or cash-segregated income
claims.mechanism: Physical constraint (only cash on hand) eliminates the cognitive burden of deciding whether to spend; the wallet becomes the de facto budget.

numbers.axis: monthly cash payment from single client

bounded_by: Method breaks down once multiple revenue streams, credit, or recurring deposits exist; does not scale beyond solo operation

claims.text: The heuristic 'if you can't buy it twice, don't buy it once' is a rule-of-thumb for filtering purchases. It is a decision gate that prevents single-high-value purchases that deplete capital, forcing prioritization of only those acquisitions that can be repeated or that compound over time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Growing business or personal wealth phase
bounded_by: The rule is aspirational, not absolute; it is stated as 'do not buy it once', not 'never buy it'

examples.text: Hormozi worked at Smoothie King making $6.75 per hour (reducing to roughly $6 per hour post-tax and fees). At lunch, he and coworkers would go to a sandwich shop next door (Kosey) and spend $13 on a sandwich, drink, and chips. Hormozi realized that $13 represented two hours of his six-hour shift, meaning he was giving away one-third of his daily earnings just for lunch. Once he framed the purchase as 'would I work two hours of my shift just to buy this sandwich?', his lunch-buying behavior stopped.

At the mall, Hormozi considered buying a $30 shirt at the Gap. He calculated that a $30 shirt represented an entire shift of work at his hourly rate. He then asked himself: 'Would I work a whole shift if someone just held up a shirt I didn't need?' The answer was no, so he did not make the purchase.

As an adult earning $100 per hour, Hormozi applies the same logic to larger purchases. A $500-1000 purchase would require 5-10 days of work. He asks: 'Would I work two days to go out with the boys for three hours on Saturday?' The answer is no, so he frames that as a reason not to make the spending choice.

practices.text: Maintain a cash-only wallet and replenish it only as income arrives; use the wallet as your de facto spending budget and avoid other payment methods (credit cards, bank transfers) that obscure the real cost of spending.
Before any purchase, convert the dollar cost into hours of work at your post-tax hourly rate, then ask yourself: would I voluntarily work that many hours just to acquire this item?
Apply the 'buy it twice' heuristic as a capital-allocation gate: only acquire items or services if you can afford to do so repeatedly or if the acquisition compounds over time.
